1 · Trigger

Mercury. Children. Autism.

Does exposure to thimerosal-containing vaccines increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder in children?

Sources: Wakefield et al., Lancet 1998;351:637-641 (MMR vaccine, not thimerosal); retraction: Lancet 2010;375:445. HHS press release, 23 Jul 2025: hhs.gov/press-room/thimerosal-mercury-removed-from-us-flu-vaccines-acip.html. ACIP vote June 2025: 5 for, 1 against, 1 abstention (press reports, e.g. STAT, 23 Jul 2025). The vote concerned flu vaccine formulation, not evidence of harm. Thimerosal is a mercury-containing preservative in multi-dose vials.
1 · Trigger

December 2025: two statements on vaccines and autism

WHO · GACVS

Statement of 11 Dec 2025

  • Two systematic reviews assessed on 27 Nov 2025
  • 31 primary studies, published Jan 2010 to Aug 2025: 16 on thiomersal, 15 on vaccines in general
  • 20 found no association. 11 suggested one, but with a high risk of bias and very low strength of evidence
  • Conclusion: vaccines, including those with thiomersal or aluminium, do not cause autism
CDC · HHS

Web page "Autism and Vaccines"

  • Changed on 19 Nov 2025 (as reported by AP)
  • Now states: "vaccines do not cause autism" is "not an evidence-based claim", because studies have not ruled out that infant vaccines cause autism
  • Cites IOM and AHRQ reviews that found "insufficient evidence"
  • The page now shows 22 Jul 2026. No reversal found (checked 2 Nov 2026)

The FDA thimerosal page (current as of 15 Jan 2025) still says 20+ years of evidence show no harm.

Sources: who.int/news/item/11-12-2025-statement-gacvs-vaccines-autism · cdc.gov/vaccine-safety/about/autism.html · AP, 20 Nov 2025 (date of change, not shown on the CDC page) · fda.gov, "Thimerosal and Vaccines"
1 · Trigger

For the room

Both agencies know the same literature. What could explain two different statements?

  • Write down your answer. Two minutes, in pairs.
  • We return to this at the end of the lecture and compare your answers with what the method can and cannot settle.
2 · What is a meta-analysis

Review, SLR, meta-analysis

Crate: review. Glass box: SLR. Sphere: meta-analysis.

Review: no stated search, no stated selection.
Example: Gerber and Offit 2009, the vaccine and autism hypotheses
Systematic literature review (SLR): a specific question, a documented search, fixed inclusion criteria, and a critical appraisal of each study.
Example: Maglione et al. 2014, routine childhood vaccines (67 studies, no pooling)
Meta-analysis: a statistical step inside an SLR. It pools the results of the included studies into one estimate, if the studies are similar enough.
Example: Taylor et al. 2014, vaccines and autism (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.06)

Other types: narrative review (no fixed method) · scoping review (maps what exists) · rapid review (shortcuts for speed) · umbrella review (a review of reviews) · living review (kept up to date) · evidence map (a visual overview of where studies exist and where the gaps are)

Sources: Definitions follow the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (ch. 1) and the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page MJ et al. BMJ 2021;372:n71, doi:10.1136/bmj.n71). Gerber JS, Offit PA. Clin Infect Dis 2009;48:456-461, doi:10.1086/596476. Maglione MA et al. Pediatrics 2014;134:325-337, doi:10.1542/peds.2014-1079. Taylor LE et al. Vaccine 2014;32:3623-3629, doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2014.04.085.
2 · What is a meta-analysis

Steps of an SLR

PROTOCOL: the methods of all six steps are written down before the search
1

Specific question

PICO / PECO.
Here: thimerosal exposure and autism in children.Tools: PROSPERO (protocol registry). Zenodo, Figshare (open repositories).

2

Search and screening

Databases, search string, two reviewers screen titles, abstracts and full texts.
Here: PubMed, 2010 to 2025.Tools: PubMed, Embase (search). Covidence, Rayyan, DistillerSR, ASReview (screening).

3

Critical appraisal

Risk of bias per study.
Here: cohort and case-control studies, e.g. Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.Tools: RoB 2, ROBINS-I, Newcastle-Ottawa (instruments). robvis (plots).

4

Summarise the results

Transparent extraction of every study into one table.
Here: design, exposure, outcome, effect size.Tools: Covidence, DistillerSR, spreadsheet.

5

Pool, if possible

Statistical pooling (meta-analysis) when studies are comparable.Tools: R (metafor), JASP, RevMan.

6

Answer the question

Conclusion with a level of evidence. Share your answer publicly.Tools: GRADEpro GDT. Open registries and repositories: PROSPERO, Zenodo, Figshare.

Sources: Steps based on the Cochrane Handbook. The "Here" and tool lines are the author's illustration and overview.
2 · What is a meta-analysis

Search: a string anyone can repeat

PICO / PECO turns the question into search terms
PPopulation: children I/EIntervention or Exposure: thimerosal-containing vaccines CComparator: no or thimerosal-free vaccines OOutcome: autism
  • Synonyms are joined with OR, concepts with AND.
  • The database itself runs the string (interface or API), once per source.
  • Same database + same string + same date = same hits. Save string, date and hit count.

AI: a language model can draft the string (synonyms, MeSH terms). It should not run the search: a chatbot is not a database and can invent or miss records. A person checks and decides.

PRESS: peer review of the search string by a second person. PRISMA-S: what to report about the search.

Each layer builds on the one below. No source covers everything: search several.

Sources: McGowan J et al. PRESS Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies: 2015 Guideline Statement. J Clin Epidemiol 2016;75:40-46. Rethlefsen ML et al. PRISMA-S: an extension to the PRISMA Statement for reporting literature searches. Syst Rev 2021;10:39. Cochrane Handbook ch. 4 (searching).
2 · What is a meta-analysis

PRISMA 2020: report what you did

  • A reporting guideline: 27 checklist items plus a flow diagram.
  • The flow diagram shows every record from search to inclusion, with reasons for exclusion.
  • It makes the selection auditable. A reader sees what was left out and why.

AI in screening: machine-learning tools such as ASReview and DistillerSR learn from your include and exclude decisions and show the most likely relevant records first. A person still decides.

Extensions exist for protocols (PRISMA-P), searches (PRISMA-S) and living reviews (PRISMA-LSR, 2024).

dummy data
Sources: Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM, et al. The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ 2021;372:n71. Flow diagram simplified and redrawn by the author. ASReview: van de Schoot R et al. Nat Mach Intell 2021;3:125-133, doi:10.1038/s42256-020-00287-7. DistillerSR: Hamel C et al. BMC Med Res Methodol 2020;20:256, doi:10.1186/s12874-020-01129-1 (simulation in 10 completed reviews: median 47% fewer records to screen at 95% recall).
2 · What is a meta-analysis

Risk of bias: how much can we trust each study?

dummy dataSix hypothetical cohort studies. They return on the next slides.

Study D is the one that finds an association, and it has high risk of bias. Does its result count the same as Study C's?

  • Judged per study, per domain, with a published tool.
  • RoB 2: randomised trials.
  • ROBINS-I: non-randomised studies.
  • Newcastle-Ottawa Scale: cohort and case-control studies.

Grey: randomised trials, not used for the vaccine and autism question.

AI: language models, for example NotebookLM working from the papers you upload, can suggest judgements, but agreement with people is limited. A person judges.

Sources: Sterne JAC et al. RoB 2. BMJ 2019;366:l4898. Sterne JAC et al. ROBINS-I. BMJ 2016;355:i4919. Wells GA et al. Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (ohri.ca). Domains simplified by the author. Judgements invented. "Association" follows the confidence intervals on the forest plot: only Study D excludes no effect (RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.33).
3 · From studies to one number

Effect measures: how a study reports its result

MeasureComparesTypical designNo effectPooled on
RR risk ratiorisk exposed / risk unexposedcohort, trial1ln(RR)
OR odds ratioodds exposed / odds unexposedcase-control1ln(OR)
HR hazard ratioevent rate over time, exposed / unexposedtime-to-event1ln(HR)
MD mean differencedifference in means, original unitscontinuous, one scale0MD itself
SMD standardised MDdifference in means, in SD unitscontinuous, different scales0SMD itself

Grey: continuous outcomes, not used for the vaccine and autism question.

Autism is recorded as a diagnosis (yes or no), so the vaccine studies report RR, OR or HR. On the ratio scale 0.5 and 2 lie unequal distances from 1, so ratios are pooled on the log scale and converted back with exp().

OR is close to RR when the outcome is rare.

Example: Taylor et al. 2014 pooled five cohort studies of vaccines and autism: OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.06).

Sources: Definitions as in the Cochrane Handbook, ch. 6 (choosing effect measures). Taylor LE et al. Vaccine 2014;32:3623-3629, doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2014.04.085.
3 · From studies to one number

Weights: precise studies count more

Large studies have narrow intervals and therefore large weights.

dummy dataThe six studies of the risk of bias slide

w = 1 / SE2

SE = [ln(upper) - ln(lower)] / 3.92

3.92 = 2 × 1.96

pooled ln RR = Σ(w × ln RR) / Σw

SE of pooled = 1 / √Σw

Transform back with exp().

Study C counts 5.5 times more than Study A.

These are fixed-effect weights. Random effects change them (two slides on).

Sources: Inverse-variance method, Cochrane Handbook ch. 10. Study A to F are the dummy set of the risk of bias slide. The percentages return in the forest plot on the next slide.
3 · From studies to one number

Reading a forest plot

dummy data Weights: see the previous slide
1
Square: the effect of one study. Its size shows the weight.
2
Horizontal line: the 95% confidence interval.
3
Dashed line: no effect (RR = 1). An interval that crosses it is compatible with no effect.
4
Diamond: the pooled estimate (fixed effect here). Its width is the pooled interval. An interval that includes 1 does not prove there is no effect.

Study D alone suggests an association: its interval does not cross 1. The pooled estimate does not.

Source: Invented numbers for six hypothetical cohort studies, drawn by the author. Not data from published studies. Layout follows the usual metafor / JASP forest plot.
3 · From studies to one number

Fixed effect versus random effects

dummy dataThe forest plot of the previous slide, now with random effects

Fixed effect: one true effect. Differences between studies are chance.

Random effects: each study has its own true effect, spread around a mean. τ² is the variance of those true effects.

Weight = 1 / (SE2 + τ2). The same τ2 is added to every study, so the weights move towards each other: Study C from 33.5% to 23.3%, Study A from 6.1% to 10.2%.

The interval becomes wider: 0.91 to 1.24 instead of 0.95 to 1.16.

I² = 54%: the share of the variation between studies that is more than chance. More on the next slide.

Sources: DerSimonian R, Laird N. Controlled Clinical Trials 1986;7:177-188 (random-effects method). Invented numbers, calculated by the author (checked in Python). τ² by DerSimonian-Laird.
3 · From studies to one number

Heterogeneity: do the studies agree?

  • I² = (Q - df) / Q. The share of the spread that is beyond chance, not how large the differences are. 25%, 50% and 75% are rough low, moderate and high.
  • Prediction interval: where the true effect of a new study may fall. It is wider than the confidence interval.
  • Q tests whether the spread is larger than chance. Low power with few studies.
  • τ²: the variance of the true effects, on the log scale.
dummy dataQ = 10.9 (df = 5), I² = 54%, τ² = 0.020

The pooled RR is 1.06, but a new study could fall anywhere between 0.68 and 1.66.

Sources: Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Deeks JJ, Altman DG. BMJ 2003;327:557-560 (I²; 25%, 50%, 75% as rough low, moderate, high). Cochrane Handbook ch. 10. Dummy data from the next slide.

4 · Trusting the result

Publication bias and the funnel plot

dummy dataA new set of 14 studies. It returns on the next slide.
  • Studies with significant results are published more often than studies without.
  • Each dot is a study: precise studies at the top, small ones at the bottom. Without bias they scatter symmetrically around the pooled effect.
  • Egger's test checks the asymmetry statistically. It needs about 10 or more studies. In this dummy set the funnel is asymmetric.

low risk of bias    high risk of bias

Asymmetry has several causes: missing studies, small studies with high risk of bias, real heterogeneity. It is a signal, not proof.

Sources: Egger M et al. BMJ 1997;315:629-634. Sterne JAC et al. BMJ 2011;343:d4002 (at least 10 studies for funnel plot tests). Invented data for 14 hypothetical studies, drawn by the author.
4 · Trusting the result

Sensitivity analysis: does the answer depend on the studies?

dummy dataThe 14 studies of the funnel plot, random effects

Sensitivity analysis: repeat the analysis with another choice, for example only the low-risk studies. Subgroup analysis: compare groups. Both are fixed in the protocol before the data are seen.

The overall result hides a difference: 1.08 for all studies, 0.99 for the low-risk studies, 1.53 for the high-risk studies.

This is the pattern behind the WHO statement: the studies that suggest an association have a high risk of bias. Here it is shown with invented data.

Risk of bias and design overlap:

cohortcase-control
low risk62
high risk15

Within the subgroups τ² = 0, so random and fixed effects agree.

Sources: Cochrane Handbook ch. 10.11. DerSimonian-Laird random effects. Invented data, constructed by the author to show the method. It does not represent the thimerosal literature.
4 · Trusting the result

GRADE: how certain are we of the pooled result?

Highfurther research is very unlikely to change the estimate
◀ randomised trials start here
Moderatefurther research is likely to have an important impact
Lowfurther research is very likely to change the estimate
◀ observational studies start here
Very lowthe estimate is very uncertain

Certainty is rated per outcome, not per study. Newer GRADE guidance lets well-appraised observational studies start higher and rates them down for risk of bias.

▼ Rate down for: risk of bias, inconsistency (heterogeneity), indirectness, imprecision, publication bias.

▲ Rate up for: a large effect, a dose-response gradient, plausible confounding that would work against the effect.

The thimerosal studies are observational, so they start at low. The WHO called the strength of evidence "very low" for the 11 studies that suggested an association (the WHO's own term).

AI: language models can draft the text. The judgement of the certainty stays with people.

dummy dataExample with the 14 dummy studies (an illustration, not a GRADE assessment). Observational: start at low. Risk of bias: serious (1.53 in high-risk studies versus 0.99 in low-risk studies). Publication bias: suspected (asymmetric funnel). Inconsistency and imprecision: not serious. Rated down to very low.
Sources: Guyatt GH et al. GRADE: an emerging consensus. BMJ 2008;336:924-926. Newer guidance: GRADE guidelines 18, J Clin Epidemiol 2019 (ROBINS-I and GRADE). Level wording shortened by the author. GRADE is a framework for judgement, not a formula.
5 · Back to the question

Why WHO and CDC differ: the same literature, a different yardstick

WHO GACVS (11 Dec 2025)CDC web page (as changed)
Question as wordedIs there evidence of a causal link between vaccines and autism?Have studies ruled out that infant vaccines cause autism?
Weighing of studiesGreatest weight on well-designed studies with low risk of bias. Little weight on studies with flaws and high risk of bias.The page describes no weighting method. It cites IOM and AHRQ reviews that found "insufficient evidence" for some vaccine and autism questions.
ConclusionThe available high-quality evidence indicates that vaccines do not cause autism."Vaccines do not cause autism" is "not an evidence-based claim", because the possibility was not ruled out.

Two things differ: how much weight a study gets, and what standard of proof the word "conclusion" needs. A meta-analysis can show the first. The second is a choice that comes before the data.

Sources: WHO GACVS statement, 11 Dec 2025. CDC, cdc.gov/vaccine-safety/about/autism.html (read 2 Nov 2026). IOM: Institute of Medicine (now National Academy of Medicine). AHRQ: US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. Wording shortened and paraphrased by the author. No judgement is made here on either agency.
5 · Back to the question

Absence of evidence and evidence of absence

dummy dataThe margin is the size of effect we want to exclude. It is chosen in advance.

WHO: evidence of absence. A narrow interval around 1 excludes relevant risks, like A. Conclusion: vaccines do not cause autism.

CDC: absence of evidence. No interval excludes every effect above zero, not even A. The possibility is not ruled out.

Same data, two questions: is a relevant effect excluded, or is any effect excluded? The data cannot choose between them. The protocol does.

One way to read both statements from the same data. The agencies do not describe it this way. No study can prove that an effect is exactly zero.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. BMJ 1995;311:485. Intervals invented by the author.
5 · Back to the question

What a meta-analysis can and cannot settle

It can

  • Give one estimate with a confidence interval, if the studies are similar enough
  • Show how much studies disagree, and why
  • Show whether the result survives without weak studies
  • Flag small-study effects

It cannot

  • Repair bias inside the included studies
  • Prove that an effect is exactly zero
  • Choose the weighting: that follows from the protocol
  • Decide what uncertainty is acceptable for policy

Back to the room: sort your answers from the start.

The studies
which studies are included (see: funnel plot)
The weighting
how much each study counts (see: risk of bias, weights, sensitivity)
The standard of proof
what "ruled out" means (see: margin)
Sources: Cochrane Handbook ch. 10 and ch. 14 (GRADE); the author's synthesis.
6 · Living

Reviews age

Schematic. The 5.5 years is the median in reviews of trials. It says nothing about whether the WHO was late.

In 100 reviews of trials (1995 to 2005): 57% got a signal that an update was needed. For 23% it came within 2 years, and 7% already had one at publication.

A signal is a change in statistical significance, a relative change of at least 50% in the effect, or a new finding on harm or caveats. It is not an error: new evidence may change the conclusion.

A static review answers the question as of its search date. Readers often use it years later.

Sources: Shojania KG et al. How quickly do systematic reviews go out of date? Ann Intern Med 2007;147:224-233 (reviews of randomised or quasi-randomised trials). WHO GACVS statement, 11 Dec 2025 (update of a 2012 review). The timeline is schematic, drawn by the author.
6 · Living

Living SLR, and a simple way to run one

  • An SLR that is kept up to date: new evidence is searched, screened and added as it appears. Each update is a new version with its own date and number.
  • PRISMA-LSR (2024) adds four reporting items to PRISMA 2020: living mode parameters, changes to methods, changes to results, and authors and their roles.
  • The protocol fixes the rules for updates before the first update.
dummy data

MosaLSR: a simple workflow for a living review

1
Protocol and sheetdecide what is collected
2
Formone html form per article, built from the sheet
3
Submissionsreviewers download a file into a shared folder
4
Import and checkfiles are checked against the sheet and logged
5
Reviewthe first author chooses where submissions differ
6
ArticleQuarto manuscript with the analysis inside

The protocol leads. It is registered on Zenodo before the work starts. Audit trail: every submission and every choice is logged, and git keeps the history.

A human decides. Screening happens outside (for example Covidence). No AI runs inside the repository.

Repository: https://github.com/MosaLSR

Sources: Elliott JH et al. Living systematic reviews: an emerging opportunity to narrow the evidence-practice gap. PLoS Med 2014;11:e1001603. PRISMA-LSR: BMJ 2024;387:e079183 (19 Nov 2024). README and docs of MosaLSR/LSR, author's summary. Version plot invented by the author.
7 · Close

Take-home

1
QuestionSpecific question (PICO) and a protocol, written before the search.
2
Search and screeningDocumented search, PRISMA flow, a reason for every exclusion.
3
AppraisalRisk of bias per study, with a published tool.
4
SummaryExtract RR and interval. Ratios are pooled on the log scale.
5
PoolingWeight by precision. Random effects adds τ². Check I², funnel plot, subgroups.
6
AnswerGRADE certainty. "Ruled out" needs a margin chosen in advance. Share it.

The same studies can lead to two statements. The difference sits in the weight a study gets and in what "ruled out" means. Decide both in the protocol, before you see the data.

AI and tools can speed up screening, extraction and drafting. A person checks and decides. A living review keeps the answer up to date.
